content:
Most of what I learn at work evaporates within a month. The fix that took a day to find, the reason a design was rejected, the one flag that makes a tool behave: gone, unless I write it down.
So this is where I’ll write it down. Some posts will be essays like this one, some will be short journal entries, and every so often there will be a longer technical write-up with code and numbers.
What to expect Posts are filed under one of three kinds, so you can follow just the ones you care about:
Blog for essays and opinions. Journal for short, dated notes on what I worked on and learned. Technical for deep dives with code, measurements, and conclusions. Each kind has its own RSS feed if you prefer to subscribe.
summary: Most of what I learn at work evaporates within a month. This blog is my attempt to keep some of it.
title: Why I Started Writing Things Down

content:
This is a sample post showing the formatting a technical write-up typically needs.
The problem A service took 14 seconds to start in staging but only 3 seconds locally.
Investigation I enabled class-loading and GC logs:
java -Xlog:class+load:file=classload.log -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log -jar app.jar Then looked for the slowest phases:
long start = System.nanoTime(); context.refresh(); log.info("Context refresh took {} ms", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000); Findings Phase Local Staging Class loading 0.8s 1.1s Bean init 1.5s 2.0s DNS lookup 0.1s 10.5s The DNS lookup was the culprit: a reverse lookup against an unreachable resolver.
Takeaways Measure before guessing. Compare environments, not just code. Write down what you ruled out, too. Tip: keep a running log of experiments while debugging. It makes the write-up almost free.
summary: A sample write-up: how I tracked down a 14-second startup, with code, logs, and a table of measurements.
title: Debugging a Slow JVM Startup
